genesis: The first book of the Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses. Genesis tells of the creation of the world, the fall of humanity in Adam and Eve, the flood in Noah's day and the tower of Babel, then follows God's covenant with Abraham and its passing to Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. It closes with Jacob's family settled in Egypt, carrying the promise that through Abraham's seed all nations will be blessed.
exodus: The second book of Moses, telling how God delivered Israel from slavery in Egypt. It recounts the call of Moses at the burning bush, the plagues, the Passover and the crossing of the Red Sea, then the giving of the Ten Commandments and the law at Mount Sinai. Its last chapters describe the building of the tabernacle, where the glory of the Lord came to dwell among His people.
leviticus: The third book of Moses, given at Sinai as Israel's manual of worship and holiness. It sets out the offerings and sacrifices, the consecration of Aaron and the priests, the laws of clean and unclean, the Day of Atonement and the yearly feasts. Its refrain is "Ye shall be holy; for I the Lord your God am holy," and Christian writers have long read its sacrifices as pictures of Christ.
numbers: The fourth book of Moses, named for the two numberings of Israel. It follows the people from Sinai through forty years in the wilderness: their murmuring, the report of the spies, the rebellion of Korah, the bronze serpent lifted up for healing, and Balaam's blessing. A generation dies in unbelief, and a new one stands on the plains of Moab ready to enter the land.
deuteronomy: The fifth book of Moses, his farewell addresses to Israel on the plains of Moab before they crossed the Jordan. Moses retells the journey from Egypt, repeats the law and calls the people to love the Lord with all their heart, soul and might. It ends with the renewal of the covenant, the song and blessing of Moses, and his death on Mount Nebo. Jesus answered the tempter three times from this book.
joshua: The book of Israel's entry into the promised land under Joshua, Moses' successor. It tells of the crossing of the Jordan, the fall of Jericho, the sin of Achan, the conquest of Canaan and the dividing of the land among the tribes. It closes with Joshua's charge to the people: "Choose you this day whom ye will serve... as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord."
judges: The history of Israel between Joshua and the rise of the kings, when "every man did that which was right in his own eyes." A repeated cycle of sin, oppression, crying out and deliverance runs through it, with God raising up judges such as Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson. Its later chapters show how far the nation fell when it forgot the Lord.
ruth: A short story set in the days of the judges. Ruth, a Moabite widow, refuses to leave her mother-in-law Naomi ("thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God") and gleans in the fields of Boaz in Bethlehem. Boaz redeems the family inheritance and marries her, and their son becomes the grandfather of King David. Christian writers have seen in Boaz a picture of Christ the kinsman-redeemer.
1-samuel: The story of Israel's passage from the judges to the kings. It begins with the birth of Samuel in answer to Hannah's prayer and his call as a boy in the temple, then tells of the people's demand for a king, the rise and fall of Saul, and the anointing of the young shepherd David, his victory over Goliath, his friendship with Jonathan and his years as a fugitive.
2-samuel: The reign of King David. It tells of his rule over Judah and then all Israel, the bringing of the ark to Jerusalem, and God's covenant promising David a house and a throne forever. It then turns to his sin with Bathsheba, Nathan's rebuke and David's repentance, and the troubles that followed in his own family, including the rebellion of Absalom.
1-kings: The history of Israel from the death of David through the divided kingdom. It tells of Solomon's wisdom and his building of the temple, his later turning to other gods, and the splitting of the kingdom into Israel and Judah. Its second half follows the prophet Elijah: the fire on Mount Carmel, the still small voice at Horeb, and his stand against Ahab and Jezebel.
2-kings: The history of the divided kingdoms to their fall. It opens with Elijah taken up in the whirlwind and Elisha's ministry of miracles, then traces the kings of Israel and Judah, good and evil, until Assyria carries Israel captive and Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple. The reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah stand out as times of turning back to the Lord.
1-chronicles: A retelling of Israel's history written after the exile, opening with genealogies from Adam to the returning exiles. Its narrative centres on David: his reign, his bringing of the ark to Jerusalem with singing, God's covenant with his house, and his preparations for the temple. It includes David's great prayer: "Thine, O Lord, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory."
2-chronicles: The history of Judah from Solomon to the exile, told with the temple and true worship at its centre. It records Solomon's dedication of the temple and God's promise, "If my people... shall humble themselves, and pray... then will I hear from heaven," and the revivals under Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah. It closes with Cyrus' decree allowing the exiles to return.
ezra: The return of the Jews from exile in Babylon. It tells how the first exiles came back under Zerubbabel and rebuilt the temple in spite of opposition, then how Ezra the priest and scribe brought a second company and taught the law of God. It ends with the people confessing and putting away their sins.
nehemiah: The memoir of Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king, who returned to rebuild the broken walls of Jerusalem. It shows him praying, planning and working under threat ("we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch") and completing the walls in fifty-two days. Ezra then reads the law to the gathered people, and a time of confession and covenant renewal follows.
esther: The story of a young Jewish woman who became queen of Persia. When Haman plots to destroy the Jews, her cousin Mordecai urges her to plead before the king: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" God is never named in the book, yet His providence runs through every turn of it. It explains the origin of the feast of Purim.
job: A poem of suffering and faith set in the patriarchal age. Job, a righteous man, loses his wealth, his children and his health, and his three friends insist he must be suffering for his sins. Job protests his innocence and longs to meet God, while still confessing "I know that my redeemer liveth." The Lord answers him out of the whirlwind, Job bows in humility, and his fortunes are restored.
psalms: The hymnbook and prayer book of Israel: one hundred and fifty songs, many attributed to David, others to Asaph, the sons of Korah, Moses and Solomon. They give voice to praise and lament, confession and trust, thanksgiving and longing for God. Christian writers have prayed and preached them more than any other book, and treasured such psalms as the 23rd, the 51st, the 91st and the 119th.
proverbs: A collection of wise sayings, most attributed to Solomon, teaching how to live well in the fear of the Lord, which is "the beginning of knowledge." It contrasts the way of wisdom and the way of folly in matters of speech, work, money, friendship, marriage and the raising of children. It closes with the portrait of the virtuous woman.
ecclesiastes: The reflections of "the Preacher," traditionally identified with Solomon, on the meaning of life under the sun. He tests pleasure, work, wealth and wisdom and finds them "vanity," fleeting and unable to satisfy. His conclusion points beyond them: "Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man."
song-of-songs: A love poem attributed to Solomon, celebrating the love between a bride and her beloved. Jewish and Christian readers alike have read it as a picture of God's love for His people, and Christian writers from Bernard of Clairvaux onward have taken it as a song of the love between Christ and His church, and between Christ and the believing soul.
isaiah: The prophecies of Isaiah in Jerusalem in the eighth century before Christ. He sees the Lord high and lifted up and cries "Woe is me," then declares judgment on Judah and the nations alongside promises of a coming king: Immanuel, the Prince of Peace. Its later chapters bring comfort to the exiles and the portrait of the suffering servant, "wounded for our transgressions," quoted throughout the New Testament.
jeremiah: The prophecies of Jeremiah, the "weeping prophet," who warned Judah for some forty years before Jerusalem fell to Babylon. Rejected, imprisoned and grieved, he called the people to repent and foretold the seventy years of exile. He also proclaimed a new covenant in which God would write His law on their hearts, a promise the New Testament sees fulfilled in Christ.
lamentations: Five poems of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah. They mourn the ruined city and its suffering people and confess that the judgment came because of sin. At their centre stands a confession of hope: "his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."
ezekiel: The prophecies of Ezekiel, a priest carried captive to Babylon. He sees visions of the glory of God, warns the exiles of Jerusalem's fall, and watches the glory depart from the temple. After the city falls, his message turns to hope: a new heart and a new spirit, the valley of dry bones brought to life, and a restored temple from which a river of life flows.
daniel: The account of Daniel and his friends, young exiles who stayed faithful to God in the court of Babylon. It tells of the fiery furnace, the writing on the wall and Daniel in the lions' den, and records his visions of the kingdoms of the world giving way to the everlasting kingdom of God and the coming of "one like the Son of man." Daniel's prayer life is a frequent theme of the classics.
hosea: The prophecies of Hosea to the northern kingdom of Israel in its last decades. God commands him to marry Gomer, who proves unfaithful, and to take her back, a living picture of the Lord's love for His unfaithful people. The book pleads with Israel to return, and promises that God will heal their backsliding and love them freely.
joel: A short prophecy sparked by a devastating plague of locusts, which Joel calls a sign of the coming day of the Lord. He calls the people to rend their hearts and not their garments, and promises restoration. Then God will pour out His Spirit on all flesh, a promise Peter declared fulfilled at Pentecost.
amos: The prophecies of Amos, a herdsman of Tekoa sent to the prosperous northern kingdom of Israel. He condemns oppression of the poor, corrupt courts and empty religious ceremony, and calls instead for justice to "run down as waters." He warns of coming judgment and exile, yet ends with the promise that the fallen tabernacle of David will be raised up.
obadiah: The shortest book of the Old Testament, a single chapter of prophecy against Edom, the nation descended from Esau. Edom had gloated over Jerusalem's fall and joined in the plunder. Obadiah announces that its pride will be brought down, and closes with the promise that "the kingdom shall be the Lord's."
jonah: The story of the prophet Jonah, sent to preach to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. He flees by sea, is thrown overboard and swallowed by a great fish, and prays from its belly until he is delivered. When he finally preaches, the whole city repents and God spares it, to Jonah's displeasure. Jesus pointed to Jonah's three days in the fish as a sign of His own death and resurrection.
micah: The prophecies of Micah, a contemporary of Isaiah, to both Israel and Judah. He denounces the greed of the powerful and the corruption of priests and prophets, and foretells judgment. He also names Bethlehem as the birthplace of the coming ruler of Israel, and sums up what the Lord requires: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God."
nahum: A prophecy of the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, the empire that had carried the northern kingdom into exile. Nahum declares the Lord slow to anger but great in power, and announces the city's destruction as good tidings to Judah. In the midst of it stands the assurance, "The Lord is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble."
habakkuk: A dialogue between the prophet Habakkuk and God. He asks why evil goes unpunished in Judah, and then why God would use the cruel Babylonians to judge it. The answer comes that "the just shall live by his faith," words that Paul quotes and that set Luther's conscience free. The book ends with a prayer of trust: "yet I will rejoice in the Lord."
zephaniah: The prophecies of Zephaniah in the reign of Josiah, announcing the great day of the Lord as a day of wrath on Judah and on the nations. He calls the humble to seek righteousness and meekness. The book ends in joy, with the Lord in the midst of His people: "he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love."
haggai: Four short messages given in 520 BC to the Jews who had returned from exile but left the temple unfinished while they built their own houses. Haggai tells them to "consider your ways," and stirs the leaders and people to resume the work. He promises that the glory of the latter house will be greater than the former.
zechariah: The prophecies of Zechariah, a contemporary of Haggai, encouraging the returned exiles to rebuild the temple. His night visions include the high priest Joshua clothed in clean garments and the word "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit." Later chapters foretell the king coming "lowly, and riding upon an ass," the thirty pieces of silver, and the one "whom they have pierced."
malachi: The last book of the Old Testament, addressed to the Jews after the return from exile. Malachi rebukes careless worship, broken marriages and the withholding of tithes, inviting the people to "prove me now herewith" and see the windows of heaven opened. He promises the coming of the Lord to His temple, preceded by a messenger, Elijah the prophet.
matthew: The first Gospel, traditionally attributed to the apostle Matthew, a former tax collector. Written with Jewish readers in view, it presents Jesus as the promised Messiah and King, often noting where the prophets are fulfilled. It gathers His teaching into great discourses, including the Sermon on the Mount and the Lord's Prayer, and ends with the Great Commission to make disciples of all nations.
mark: The shortest Gospel, traditionally attributed to John Mark, a companion of Peter. Brisk and vivid, it moves quickly from one deed of Jesus to the next, showing Him as the Son of God who came "not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." Nearly a third of the book is given to the last week of His life, His death and resurrection.
luke: The Gospel written by Luke, the physician and companion of Paul, as an orderly account for Theophilus. It gives the fullest story of Jesus' birth and childhood, and many parables found nowhere else, including the good Samaritan and the prodigal son. It shows Christ's compassion for the poor, the outcast and the sinner, and closes with the resurrection and ascension.
john: The fourth Gospel, traditionally attributed to the apostle John, "the disciple whom Jesus loved." It opens with the Word who was with God and was God, made flesh, and is built around signs and the "I am" sayings of Jesus. Its long account of the upper room, with Christ's teaching on the Comforter and His prayer for His disciples, has fed devotional writers more than almost any other passage.
acts: The second volume of Luke's work, telling how the gospel spread from Jerusalem to Rome. It begins with the ascension and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, follows Peter and the church in Jerusalem, the death of Stephen and the conversion of Saul, and then traces Paul's missionary journeys. The classics return to it constantly as the pattern of Spirit-filled life and witness.
romans: Paul's letter to the church at Rome, the fullest statement of the gospel in the New Testament. It shows that all have sinned and that God justifies sinners by faith in Christ, apart from the works of the law. It goes on to life in the Spirit, the assurance that nothing can separate us from the love of God, God's purposes for Israel, and the practical life of a living sacrifice.
1-corinthians: Paul's letter to the church he had planted at Corinth, a gifted but divided and worldly congregation. He addresses factions, immorality, lawsuits, marriage, food offered to idols, the Lord's Supper and spiritual gifts, answering each from the cross of Christ. It contains the great chapter on love and the fullest New Testament teaching on the resurrection of the body.
2-corinthians: Paul's most personal letter, written to Corinth after a painful visit and a severe letter. He defends his ministry against false apostles, and speaks of comfort in affliction, treasure in earthen vessels, and the ministry of reconciliation. He writes of his thorn in the flesh and the Lord's answer, "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
galatians: Paul's urgent letter to the churches of Galatia, who were being persuaded that Gentile believers must keep the law of Moses to be saved. He insists that a man is justified by faith in Christ, not by works of the law, and calls them to stand fast in the liberty with which Christ has made them free. It describes the fruit of the Spirit, and Luther called it his own letter.
ephesians: Paul's letter, written from prison, on the church in God's eternal purpose. It unfolds every spiritual blessing in Christ, salvation by grace through faith, and the joining of Jew and Gentile in one body. Paul prays that believers may know the love of Christ, then turns to life in the church, marriage and the home, and the whole armour of God.
philippians: Paul's warm letter of thanks to the church at Philippi, written from prison. Joy runs through it in spite of his chains. He sets before them the mind of Christ, who humbled Himself to the death of the cross, counts all things loss to know Christ, and tells them to be anxious for nothing but bring everything to God in prayer. "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me."
colossians: Paul's letter to the church at Colossae, warning against a teaching that added philosophy, ceremonies and angel worship to Christ. He answers with the supremacy of Christ, the image of the invisible God, in whom dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. Believers are complete in Him, and are to set their affections on things above.
1-thessalonians: One of Paul's earliest letters, written to a young church facing persecution soon after he had to leave it. He gives thanks for their faith and love, urges them to holiness, and comforts them about believers who have died with the hope of the Lord's return. Among its short commands: "Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks."
2-thessalonians: Paul's second letter to Thessalonica, written to correct the idea that the day of the Lord had already come. He encourages them under persecution with the justice of God, describes events that must come first, including the man of sin, and rebukes those who had stopped working, saying that "if any would not work, neither should he eat."
1-timothy: Paul's letter to Timothy, his son in the faith, left to lead the church at Ephesus. It gives instruction on prayer, the qualifications of overseers and deacons, the care of widows, and guarding sound doctrine against false teachers. It contains the saying "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief," and the charge to "fight the good fight of faith."
2-timothy: Paul's last letter, written from prison in Rome as he expected death. He urges Timothy to stir up the gift of God, to endure hardship as a good soldier, to rightly divide the word of truth, and to preach the word in season and out of season. It holds his testimony, "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith."
titus: Paul's letter to Titus, left in Crete to set the churches in order. It gives the qualifications of elders and instructions for older and younger believers and servants, so that sound doctrine may be adorned by godly living. Its summary of the gospel speaks of the grace of God that brings salvation and teaches us to live soberly, righteously and godly.
philemon: A short personal letter from Paul to Philemon, a believer at Colossae, about his runaway slave Onesimus, who had been converted through Paul in prison. Paul sends him back, asking Philemon to receive him "not now as a servant, but... a brother beloved," and offers to pay whatever he owes. It has long been read as a picture of Christ's intercession for sinners.
hebrews: A letter of unknown authorship to Jewish believers tempted to turn back from Christ. It shows Christ as better than angels, Moses and the priesthood of Aaron: the great High Priest who offered Himself once for all and opened the way into the holiest. Its eleventh chapter recalls the heroes of faith, and it calls readers to run with patience, "looking unto Jesus."
james: A practical letter from James, traditionally identified as the brother of the Lord and leader of the church in Jerusalem. It teaches joy in trials, asking God for wisdom, taming the tongue and caring for the poor, and insists that "faith without works is dead." It closes with the prayer of faith, and with Elijah as an example of the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man.
1-peter: The apostle Peter's letter to believers scattered through Asia Minor and suffering for their faith. He reminds them of their living hope and their calling as a holy priesthood, a people for God's own possession. He teaches submission and patient endurance after the example of Christ, and the call to cast all their care upon Him, "for he careth for you."
2-peter: Peter's final letter, written as he expected death. He urges believers to add virtue, knowledge, temperance, patience, godliness, brotherly kindness and love to their faith, and appeals to his own witness of the transfiguration. He warns against false teachers and scoffers who deny the Lord's return, assuring that the Lord is not slack concerning His promise.
1-john: A letter of the apostle John to churches troubled by false teachers who denied that Christ had come in the flesh. It is written "that ye may know that ye have eternal life," giving tests of true faith in obedience, love for the brethren and belief in Christ. It declares that "God is light" and that "God is love," and that the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin.
2-john: A brief letter from "the elder" to "the elect lady and her children," usually taken to be a church and its members. It calls them to walk in truth and love, keeping the commandment to love one another, and warns them not to receive deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.
3-john: A short personal letter from "the elder" to his friend Gaius. He commends Gaius for walking in the truth and for his hospitality to travelling preachers, contrasts the domineering Diotrephes, who refused to receive them, and praises Demetrius. It opens with the wish that Gaius may prosper and be in health, even as his soul prospers.
jude: A brief letter from Jude, traditionally identified as the brother of James. He urges believers to "earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints" against ungodly men who had crept in and turned grace into licence. It ends with one of the best-loved doxologies of Scripture: "Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling."
revelation: The last book of the Bible, the revelation of Jesus Christ given to John in exile on the island of Patmos. It opens with letters from Christ to seven churches, then shows the throne of God, the Lamb that was slain, and visions of judgment on the world and the defeat of evil. It closes with the new heaven and new earth, where God wipes away every tear, and the promise "Surely I come quickly."
